summary: libp2p: gossipsub creates a permanent topics-map entry per distinct subscription with no cap in the default config
description:
### Summary
A single gossipsub peer can grow a node's `topics` map without bound by flooding subscription RPCs, because the default configuration has no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap and peer scoring does not penalise subscription volume. The peer is never greylisted, so the growth continues toward OOM.

### Details
`handleReceivedSubscription` (`packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts:1028`, line 1036) runs `this.topics.set(topic, new Set())` for every distinct topic string:

```ts
private handleReceivedSubscription (from, topic, subscribe) {
  let topicSet = this.topics.get(topic)
  if (subscribe) {
    if (topicSet == null) {
      topicSet = new Set()
      this.topics.set(topic, topicSet)   // no global cap, no per-peer cap
    }
    topicSet.add(from.toString())
  }
}
```

The only topical gate (`gossipsub.ts:981`, `if (this.allowedTopics != null && !this.allowedTopics.has(topic)) return`) is skipped when `allowedTopics` is null — the default. Subscriptions are unsigned RPC metadata (no signature needed); `decodeRpc`'s per-RPC limit caps count (`maxSubscriptions = 5000`) but not topic-string length or aggregate size; and the peer-scoring components P1–P7 have no subscription-volume term, so the attacker's score stays at 0 (above the `graylistThreshold` of −80) and `acceptFrom` keeps returning true. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/gossipsub` reads `16.0.4`.

### PoC
Full PoC attached (`gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz`). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (`npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build`), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of `packages/`), then `cd gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc && node attack.mjs`. Expected (default config):

```
[*] sending 300 RPC frames x 4000 unique ~190-byte topic subscriptions (1,200,000 topics total)
[*]   progress: 88% sent | victim topics=1,032,000 rss=740MB peers=1
[*] victim quiesced: topics=~1,100,000 rss=~870MB peers=1
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: one connected peer grew the victim's gossipsub topics map to ~1.1M entries (RSS +~900MB) with 300 subscription RPCs — no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap in the default config
```

Control run (`ALLOWED_TOPICS=legit-topic`, i.e. `node attack.mjs control`): the identical flood is rejected at the `allowedTopics` gate and the topics map stays at 0 entries — confirming the vulnerable condition is the default `allowedTopics`-unset config. The map grows monotonically with no cap until the victim's own resource pressure trips; on disconnect `removePeer` performs an O(N) sweep over every topic entry (a secondary CPU cost) while the ~1 GB heap stays committed.

### Impact
CWE-400/CWE-770. Every node running default gossipsub is affected; the attacker needs only one connection and is never rate-limited or greylisted. Growth continues toward OOM; on disconnect the O(N) `removePeer` sweep adds CPU cost. Suggested fix: bound by default (not opt-in) — a global cap on `topics.size`, a per-peer subscription cap with a P7 behaviour penalty so `acceptFrom` eventually greylists, a topic-string length cap at decode time, and/or flipping `allowedTopics` to deny-by-default; make `removePeer`'s topic iteration non-blocking/capped.

[gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30452451/gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz)

summary: libp2p: ASN.1 DER decoder drives an unbounded synchronous loop on attacker-controlled length fields, stalling the Node event loop pre-auth
description:
### Summary
A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted `publicKey` inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

### Details
`packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts` `readLength()` parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to `buf.byteLength`, and `readInteger()` then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

```ts
function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}
```

The blob reaches the parser pre-auth: Identify runs on every `connection:open` and calls `publicKeyFromProtobuf(publicKey)` (`packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts:85`) before the `connection.remotePeer.equals(id)` check at `identify.ts:88`. The `MAX_RSA_JWK_SIZE` guard in `pkixToRSAPublicKey` only bounds the total blob size, not the inner length field, so a 15-byte payload defeats it; the ECDSA path (`unmarshalECDSAPublicKey`) has no cap at all. The decode runs in a single synchronous tick, so no `AbortSignal` — including Identify's 5 s timeout — can interrupt it. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/crypto` reads `5.1.21`.

### PoC
Full PoC attached (`libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz`). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (`npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build`), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of `packages/`), then `cd libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc && node attack.mjs`. Expected:

```
[*] round 1: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 2: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4-5s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 3: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: 3/3 connections each stalled the victim's event loop for ~4-5s — one crafted ~15-byte Identify publicKey per connection, pre-auth
```

The stall is measured from the victim's own 1 s heartbeat clock (frozen while the loop is blocked); the ~2 GB transient RSS peak is read from `/proc/<pid>/status`. The DER `RangeError` is swallowed by Identify's `.catch(() => {})`, so the node survives and every new connection re-stalls it; under a container memory limit the ~2 GB spike OOM-kills the process. A `node attack.mjs control` run (legitimate Identify) shows 0 s stalls.

### Impact
CWE-130/CWE-400. Any node running the default Identify service is affected. A single peer can keep the node unresponsive to all of its peers (every new connection adds another multi-second stall — all timers, heartbeats, and protocol timeouts stop) and, in memory-constrained deployments, force an OOM kill. Suggested fix: in `readLength`, reject any long-form length whose value exceeds `buf.byteLength - context.offset`; in `readInteger`/`readObjectIdentifier`/`readBitString`/`readOctetString`, clamp or assert `end`/`finalOffset` against `buf.byteLength` before looping; add an overall DER-element-length sanity cap at `decodeDer` entry and a byte-length cap in `unmarshalECDSAPublicKey`.

[libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30452369/libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz)

summary: Filament Curator: Cross-tenant media metadata disclosure via Curator picker search
description:
Summary

  In multitenant Filament panels, an authenticated user could retrieve media metadata belonging to other tenants
  by typing in the Curator media-picker search box. The search query omitted the tenant ownership scope that the
  normal file listing applies.

  Details

  CuratorPanel::updatedSearch() built its Eloquent query independently of getFiles() and did not apply the
  filament()->hasTenancy() && $isTenantAware tenant-ownership where clause. As a result, the search matched media
  across all tenants. A secondary flaw compounded it: the orWhere('title'…) chain was not wrapped in a nested
  group, so the OR conditions also broke out of the isLimitedToDirectory constraint.

  The issue was introduced in v3.2.4, when multitenancy support was added to the media picker.

  Impact

  - Who: any authenticated user with access to a panel that uses the Curator picker.
  - What: disclosure of other tenants' media metadata (name, title, alt, caption, description, path, etc.)
  returned by the search.
  - Conditions: only affects deployments using Filament multitenancy with Curator's tenant awareness enabled.
  Single-tenant installs are not affected.

  Patches

  Fixed in 3.7.8, 4.1.1, and 5.1.1 by applying the tenant scope to the search query and grouping the search terms
  so they cannot escape the directory/tenant constraints. Upgrade to a patched version.

  Workarounds

  None other than upgrading. Disabling tenant awareness does not help (it removes the boundary entirely).

  Credit

  Reported via coordinated disclosure by [Afsana Alijabarova](https://github.com/afa114).

summary: qbee-agent: Local Privilege Escalation and Arbitrary File Tampering via Symlink Following in createFile helper
description:
This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

### Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

1. **Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration)**: If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own `~/.ssh` directory and create a symlink pointing to `/root/.ssh`. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like `fs.protected_symlinks` do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

2. **Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging)**: On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (`/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part`). If `fs.protected_symlinks` is disabled `(0)`, an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/pam.d/*`), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

3. **Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution)**: If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute `file.Chown()` on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside `app/configuration/file_manager.go`. Specifically, the agent now enforces `syscall.O_NOFOLLOW` and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

### Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

1. Disable the SSH Keys Bundle: Temporarily turn off SSH key management within the Qbee platform for non-trusted local accounts to eliminate the primary privilege escalation vector.

2. Restrict Local Home Directory Alterations: Enforce strict file permissions or monitoring on managed user home directories to block unprivileged users from deleting or replacing ~/.ssh with a symbolic link.

3. Enable Kernel Symlink Protection: Ensure that system-level symlink protections are active to mitigate the secondary `/tmp` vector by verifying that the following sysctl parameter is set to 1 (though note this does not fix the primary home directory vector):

```bash
sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1
```

AWS-advanced-jdbc-wrapper: Java Deserialization RCE via Cache Poisoning
description:
### Impact
The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source JDBC driver wrapper that extends a JDBC driver to enable Amazon Aurora and AWS Cloud features such as failover handling and caching. We identified CVE-2026-14265, an issue in the RemoteQueryCachePlugin of the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper. When this plugin is enabled, query results read from the shared Redis/Valkey cache are deserialized without class filtering. An actor with write access to the shared cache infrastructure could insert a crafted serialized Java object that, when read by an application, results in execution of arbitrary code on the application server.

### Workarounds
The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by disabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, and by restricting write access to the Redis/Valkey cache infrastructure to trusted principals.

summary: pympp allows excessive sponsored transaction fees through padded calldata
description:
### Details
When the server acts as the fee_payer, `pympp` 0.8.0 validates calldata using `eth_abi` decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The `FeePayerPolicy` caps `gas_limit` (≤ 2 M) and `max_fee_per_gas` (≤ 100 Gwei) but does **not** check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: **16 gas per non-zero byte**. Appending `N` bytes of `0x01` padding inflates actual gas used by `N × 16` while keeping `gas_limit` and `max_fee_per_gas` within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

**Vulnerable code path:** `FeePayerPolicy` in `fee_payer_policy.py` (pympp 0.8.0) enforces `maxGas = 2_000_000` and `maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei` but has no `calldata.length` bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared `gas_limit`.

**Note:** In our experiment, we enforce an 16 KB `max_header_length`, which caps the maximum effective padding at roughly 5,500 bytes. The default padding in this PoC (5,500 bytes) is within that limit.

### PoC
The PoC is provided below. It is configured to reproduce the attack on Tempo Moderate testnet within a Docker environment. Download the PoC and run:
```bash
unzip pympp_python_PoC.zip
cd pympp_python
docker build -t pympp-padding .
docker run --rm pympp-padding
``` 
There are more details in `pympp_python/README.md`

### Impact
In our experiment, a malicious client can force the server to pay ~**5x** the normal transaction fee. This dramatically increases operational costs and completely destroys the profit margin on low-cost items.

Please provide a way to share the PoC in .zip format to you. Thank you!

summary: Phoenix: Format String Injection in applyChatTemplate
description: - Summary A format string injection vulnerability in the applyChatTemplate GraphQL endpoint allows an attacker to read server-side environment variables, cryptographic secrets, and internal module attributes directly from the API response. On default Phoenix installations where authentication is disabled the endpoint is reachable with no credentials. On auth-enabled deployments, any account regardless of privilege level is sufficient to exploit it. - Impact Server filesystem paths, loaded Python module names, and internal configuration constants are fully disclosed, an attacker with network access can read the full server `os.environ` including the admin credentials hardcoded in `phoenix.auth`. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to extract PHOENIX_SECRET, the master key used to sign all JWTs and derive the Fernet encryption key protecting stored credentials (LLM API keys, OAuth tokens). With this key, an attacker can forge admin-level session tokens and decrypt all secrets stored in the database. - Affected Versions First vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v13.0.0 (2026-02-13) Latest confirmed vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v14.8.0 (2026-04-17) - Affected Component `applyChatTemplate` GraphQL query endpoint (`src/phoenix/server/api/queries.py:1638`) `FStringTemplateFormatter._format()` template rendering function (`src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:272`) `DotDict.__getattr__()` ineffective attribute access control (`src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:90`) - Proof of Concept payload as txt with an image performing the exploit below. - Payload: ``` { "query": "query($t: PromptChatTemplateInput!, $o: PromptTemplateOptions!) { applyChatTemplate(template: $t, templateOptions: $o) { messages { content { ... on TextContentPart { text { text } } } } } }", "variables": { "t": { "messages": [{ "role": "USER", "content": [{ "text": { "text": "{u.__class__.__bases__[0].__init__.__globals__[_os].environ}" } }] }] }, "o": { "format": "F_STRING", "variables": { "u": { "x": 1 } } } } } ``` - Suggested Fix Three mitigations are recommended in combination: restrict attribute traversal at the Formatter.get_field() level (not the wrapper class), add IsAuthenticated permission to the applyChatTemplate resolver, and limit F_STRING format to trusted system-defined templates only. Best Regards, Omar

summary: Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata
description:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer `'use cache'` function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner `'use cache'` call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via `next/root-params`) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.
